Caissa, the chess engine Gambit plays (its computer players, its coach and the review of a finished game), built from
source as a single-threaded WebAssembly module, with its neural network.

Source:   https://github.com/Witek902/Caissa, commit 324f1f903eadbb889180e7b0b097af5fa6748f44 (19 October 2026, version
          2.0.12), by Michal Witanowski
Changes:  caissa-wasi.patch, applied to that commit: no thread is started (a search runs to its end inside the call,
          so every search needs a limit), the UCI loop takes its commands one at a time from the page's worker instead
          of standard input, no tablebase file is looked for, the transposition table starts at 16 MB, and the network
          is not read from a file: the worker asks the engine for room (net_alloc), copies the bytes in and calls
          net_ready, so its 76 MB are held once. The entry points are uci_init, uci_buffer, uci_command, net_size,
          net_alloc, net_ready. No rule, search or evaluation is changed. wasi-shim/ stands in for what a WebAssembly
          C++ library leaves out: <thread>, <mutex> and <condition_variable> (the engine's search threads never start),
          and <immintrin.h>, the ~25 x86 SSE instructions the network code uses, written over WebAssembly SIMD with
          the same arithmetic (the evaluations of the WebAssembly build and a native x86-64 build of the commit are the
          same number for number). WebAssembly SIMD needs Safari 16.4 / iOS 16.4 or later.
Build:    build.sh (clang 18 for wasm32-wasi, with the WASI C library and libc++ from Ubuntu's wasi-libc and
          libc++-18-dev-wasm32 packages; the C++ library and the C library are linked into the .wasm, under the
          Apache 2.0 licence with the LLVM exception and the MIT and public-domain terms of wasi-libc, none of which
          asks for more than they already get from being named here). The script rebuilds caissa.wasm byte for byte
          (SHA-256 9c877c0fa77967c7eb34c6af982bc303fbfdd2a04978ba9fd3994ae73f3f1e15, 262,942 bytes).
Network:  eval-ml-11a-100B-spsa-transplant.pnn, the network the commit's makefile downloads, from
          https://github.com/Witek902/Caissa-Nets (a release of that name; commit 513b990ddb1204ca25a650cfb8d31e13b38a9414),
          75,703,872 bytes, SHA-256 bc3df8d32b584f01e21f0f3f9515b3fc0f97fa0ca59b9b5991f333ed5b437b6b: 32 king buckets x
          768 features into 1,536 int16 neurons, then 1536 -> 16 -> 32 -> 1 in int8, 8 variants by piece count. Trained
          by the author on the engine's own self-play positions (20.5 billion, per the README).
          caissa.pnn.z is that file, losslessly packed for the page by pack-net.mjs (the feature transformer's low bytes,
          then its high bytes, then the rest, deflated raw: 37.7 MB; SHA-256 1fae1122eceec2460157138317e56c069e680182056102e2c6d3e70791d0954e), and unpacked by
          fillNet() in gambit-caissa.js into the engine's memory byte for byte (tests/gambit-engine.mjs checks the
          search it then plays, which any changed byte would move).
Licence:  Caissa: MIT (LICENSE-Caissa.txt). The network: the Caissa-Nets repository carries no licence file of its own.
          The author releases the engine under the MIT licence and its build downloads this network by itself and
          puts it beside the binary, so the network is used here as the author distributes it; but nothing says so in
          words. Asking the author to add a licence file to Caissa-Nets (or to say in the engine's README that the
          nets are MIT as well) settles it. Until then Arasan (MIT, network included, licence file in its repository)
          is the fallback; see docs/licences-images-and-engines.md.

Why not the Stockfish this replaced: GPL v3 (docs/licences-images-and-engines.md). Why not kishi: MIT and already
WebAssembly, but about 2,000 Elo, below Gambit's strongest levels.
